Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Old Memories: Old photos, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Sarah, a 39-year-old dentist, remembered the day her life irrevocably shifted with stark clarity. It began as a sudden, aggressive autoimmune flare that rapidly progressed, leaving her gasping for breath and critically ill. Weeks blurred into a terrifying ordeal in the intensive care unit, intubated and utterly dependent. She recalled the suffocating feeling of being unable to move, unable to speak, her decisions made by others, her body a battlefield she had no control over. Even after the immediate crisis passed, the long, arduous recovery left her physically diminished, grappling with a profound sense of having been utterly betrayed by her own physiology. She had come to believe, with a chilling certainty, that she could no longer trust her own body; it had proven itself unreliable, a fragile vessel prone to turning against her without warning.

In the months that followed, echoes of that terrifying experience began to intrude on her daily life. The clean, sterile scent of antiseptic, ubiquitous in her dental practice, became a potent reminder of the hospital, sending a jolt of panic through her. When a patient, particularly one with complex needs, required her full, sustained attention, she would sometimes feel a familiar dread creep in—the sensation of being physically constrained, unable to disengage, an echo of the entrapment she felt in the ICU. She found herself struggling to maintain her focus during long procedures, her heart pounding as the scent of sterile wipes permeated the air, or if she felt unable to take a break when she needed one. Even innocuous moments could be triggers; recently, while sorting through old photo albums with her partner, an image of herself from before her illness, vibrant and carefree, brought a wave of despair. It was a painful reminder of the person she felt she no longer was, solidifying her belief that she had permanently changed for the worse, becoming a weaker, diminished version of her former self.

To cope, Sarah developed an intricate web of strategies. She began to actively avoid looking at or paying attention to her own body. She stopped checking herself for any new aches or unusual sensations, avoiding mirrors and even steering clear of clothing that might draw attention to her physical form. This was her way of trying to outrun the constant fear that her body would once again betray her. Socially, she started to pull back, declining invitations from friends and even making excuses to avoid larger family gatherings. The thought of engaging in casual conversation felt draining, and the possibility of someone asking about her illness was enough to make her heart race. She found herself increasingly avoiding other people, preferring the quiet solitude of her home. Most significantly, she avoided talking with anyone, even her partner, about the traumatic event or its lingering aftermath. The words felt lodged in her throat, too heavy, too terrifying to articulate, and she feared that speaking about it would only make the terrifying reality more concrete, or worse, expose her perceived weakness.

This avoidance, however, had its own consequences. At work, the constant vigilance against triggers made her already demanding job as a dentist feel exhausting. She found herself taking more frequent, albeit brief, breaks, stepping out of the treatment room to escape the antiseptic smell, which sometimes led to minor delays in her schedule. Her partner, initially patient and understanding, had started to express concern and frustration about her increasing withdrawal and her refusal to discuss what she was going through. Sarah knew she was pushing him away, but the thought of opening up felt like standing at the edge of a precipice. What frightened her most was the idea that if she allowed herself to acknowledge the depth of her fear and the extent of her perceived weakness, she might truly shatter. It was this growing isolation, the strain on her relationship, and the relentless anxiety that finally compelled her to seek help, hoping for a way to reclaim some semblance of the life she felt had been stolen from her.
